opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's honestly one of the hardest open questions for us right now. With a standard video generation model you can lean on things like FVD or human ratings of visual quality, and those are useful, but they miss what makes an interactive model interesting: does it actually respond to what you do?

So I tend to think about it along a few axes. The first is controllability. If I press "jump" or "move left," does the world change the way I'd expect, and does it do so consistently? One approach is to look at how much the generated frames differ when you condition on different actions versus the same action. If the model ignores the action and produces roughly the same video regardless, that's a sign it's basically a video model and not a world model.

The second is consistency over time. Interactive models get rolled out autoregressively, so small errors compound. You can have something that looks great for a second or two and then drifts: objects disappear, the layout changes when you turn around and come back. So we look at how quality and coherence hold up over longer horizons, and whether the model remembers things that went out of view.

The third, which I think matters most in the long run, is usefulness downstream. If the goal is to train agents in these generated worlds, then the real test is whether an agent trained or evaluated inside the model behaves sensibly, and whether that transfers back to real environments. That's much more expensive to measure, but it's closer to what we actually care about.

And then there's a human side. You can just put people in front of it and let them play. You learn a lot quickly that way: whether it feels responsive, whether it's fun, where it breaks. It's not a scalable metric, but it's often the most honest signal we have.

Overall I'd say the field doesn't have a single agreed-upon benchmark yet, and I think building good evaluations for interactivity is as important as building the models themselves.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts established video-quality measures with the harder open question of evaluating interactivity, then identifies controllability—whether actions produce expected changes—as a key measure.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because it's actually a really hard problem. When you're evaluating a generative model that produces an image or a video, you can sort of look at a single sample and ask, does this look realistic, does it match the prompt. But with an interactive model, the whole point is that the output depends on what you do. So you take an action, the model responds, you take another action based on that, and now you've got this whole trajectory that's a product of both the model and the agent interacting with it. A single frame doesn't tell you much.

So I tend to break it down into a few pieces. One is fidelity, which is basically, does it look right? And there you can borrow from the video generation world, things like FVD, perceptual metrics, that sort of thing. But that's only part of the story. The second piece, and honestly the one I care about most, is controllability. If I press left, does the thing actually go left? And does it go left consistently? Because a model can produce beautiful, totally plausible video that just ignores your actions, and that's not an interactive model, that's a video model with extra inputs.

The way we've tried to get at controllability is by actually probing the model with actions. So you take the same starting state, you feed it different actions, and you ask how different are the resulting outcomes. If the actions don't matter, the outcomes converge and that's a red flag. Or you can go the other direction and try to infer the action from a pair of consecutive frames the model generated, and see how well that lines up with what you actually put in. That gives you something quantitative, but you have to be careful because you can get a high score there and still have a model that feels terrible to play with.

And that's the third thing, which is that at some point you have to put a human in the loop, or at least an agent in the loop. Interactivity is kind of inherently experiential. Does it stay coherent over time? Does it remember that there was a wall there ten steps ago? Does it feel responsive? Some of that you can proxy with long-horizon consistency metrics, but a lot of it right now really comes down to having people interact with it and report what they experience. And then, if you're thinking about these models as environments for training agents, there's a very practical downstream metric, which is, does an agent trained in the learned environment actually transfer to the real one? That's in some ways the most honest test, because it doesn't care whether the pixels are pretty, it cares whether the dynamics are right.

So I'd say the short answer is there isn't one number. It's a combination of visual quality, action consistency, long-horizon coherence, and then some grounding in either human judgment or downstream utility. And I think the field is still figuring out how to weight those.

r001.rationale: The response says evaluating interactive models is hard and describes controllability metrics, but it does not clearly state that controllability is harder to measure than video quality.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that you’re measuring a system that’s interacting with something, so its predictions influence what happens next. You can’t necessarily capture that with accuracy on a fixed dataset. You want to understand how well it accomplishes the task over the course of an interaction, and whether it can recover when something goes wrong.

If it’s interacting with a person, that also raises the question of what success means for that person. Does the model help them achieve their goal? How much feedback or intervention do they have to provide? A model might do well on a task metric but still be frustrating to work with. So I’d look at both the outcome and the process of getting there, across different users and situations.

r001.rationale: The response discusses task success, recovery, user effort, and interaction quality, but it does not compare controllability with video quality or say controllability is harder to measure.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that you can’t really evaluate an interactive model in isolation. Its actions affect what it observes next, so you need to look at how it performs over the course of an interaction. Does it actually accomplish the task? How much interaction does it need to get there? And how well does it recover when something unexpected happens?

For a reinforcement learning agent, you might measure cumulative reward or task success, but those numbers depend on what you’ve chosen to reward and the conditions you test under. So I’d also want to understand whether it generalizes to new situations. Has it learned a useful behavior, or has it just found something that works in a very particular environment?

r001.rationale: The response discusses task success, interaction cost, recovery, and generalization, but does not compare measuring controllability with measuring video quality or say that controllability is harder to measure.
